episodes.title: The Path to a Democratic Supermajority
episodes.description: Democrats are on track to have more power in the next Congress than they’ve had since 2009. How can they navigate the divides in a party that now stretches from Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan to Adam...
episodes.description_full:
Democrats are on track to have more power in the next Congress than they’ve had since 2009. How can they navigate the divides in a party that now stretches from Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan to Adam Hamilton in Kansas? How do they prevent all their new voters in this election from flipping back in the next one? Can they turn this victory into a springboard to an even bigger and more durable Democratic majority in 2028 and beyond?

We will have two episodes that try to answer these questions from different angles, one from the center of the party and one from the left. First, representing the more center view, we have Adam Jentleson, the founder and president of the Searchlight Institute, a Washington think tank. Jentleson is a veteran of the Senate; he served as deputy chief of staff to the former Senate majority leader Harry Reid and chief of staff to Senator John Fetterman. He’s also the author of two books, “Kill Switch: The Rise of the Modern Senate and the Crippling of American Democracy,” and  “Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power,” which came out in September.

episodes.description_full: The band Mastodon formed in 2000 in Atlanta, Georgia. They’ve won a Grammy and been nominated for 5 others, and three of their albums have debuted at #1 on Billboard’s Hard Rock charts. For most of their history, they were a four piece, made up of Brann Dailor, Troy Sanders, Bill Kelliher, and Brent Hinds. But in March 2025, Brent Hinds left the band. And later that year, he died in a motorcycle accident. For this episode, I spoke to Brann, Troy, and Bill about making the song “Your Ghost Again,” which came together in the wake of Brent’s death, and the death of Brann’s mother. Along with their new members, Nick Johnston and João Nogueira, they released their 9th album, Marrow Deep, in August 2026. I went to their studio in Atlanta, and talked to them about everything they went through and everything that went into the song “Your Ghost Again.” For more info, visit songexploder.net/mastodon.

episodes.description_full: Reversing aging may sound like science fiction, but scientists have already found a way to do it—at least, theoretically. Based on a 2012 Nobel-prize winning discovery, researchers are testing whether they can revert diseased cells in the eye back to young and healthy ones. They gave people a drug this year. If it works, it’ll open the door to curing and possibly preventing other age-related diseases. And that led producer Berly McCoy to wonder: Could all this research eventually extend our human lifespans? If you like this episode, check out our episodes on zombie cells, why our hair turns gray and why we die.Interested in more science on aging? episodes.description_full:
President Trump is primarily responsible for the Republican shellacking on Tuesday. But to get over the finish line in so many places — across the Midwest and deep into the South – Democrats had to run the right candidates, and those candidates ran very different campaigns.

So how exactly did those Democrats do it? Michelle Goldberg, my colleague at New York Times Opinion, did amazing work this past year covering the biggest races — traveling to Texas, Michigan, Maine and other states, meeting with the candidates, and getting a sense of their campaigns on the ground. She joins me for a deep dive into the most exciting — and shocking — wins, and what they reveal about the new Democratic Party that will emerge out of this election.

episodes.description_full:
“I’m pragmatic,” Hasan Piker says, when it comes to how Democrats wield power.

Our last episode of the show featured a more centrist perspective on what Democrats should learn from their midterm triumph and what they should do when they take control of Congress next year. Today, we wanted to pair that with a perspective from the left.

Piker might be the most prominent leftist commentator in politics right now. The popular Twitch streamer catapulted to main character status in the recent election cycle, as he took on a more hands-on role stumping for candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and the right tried to turn him into a boogeyman in response.

So I want to talk to Piker about the election and how the Democratic Party should act going forward — especially when it comes to health reform, where I see a synthesis coming into view, and Israel, the issue where Piker is the most personally controversial, and where the Democratic coalition is at the greatest risk of tearing apart.

episodes.description_full: At the end of October, seemingly overnight, a major law firm called Weil Gotshal announced it was winding down after a number of partners departed and talks of a merger with another firm failed. So how did a $2 billion big law firm collapse in the span of a few weeks? In 2015, Yale Law professor John Morley published a paper called "Why Law Firms Collapse," that now looks very prescient, with his idea of a “partner run," or the law firm version of a bank run. What is especially interesting about Morley's paper is his forensic examination of partner-led businesses and the idea that the model might be inherently fragile. In this episode, we talk to Morley about his newly relevant paper, the collapse of Weil Gotshal, whether AI will really change how law firms are run, and the future of big law. On this episode, we talk to Hawkins about how she and our Bloomberg News colleagues began investigating Megaspeed and its relationship to Nvidia, the raging debate in Washington over chip export controls, and the incredibly sophisticated and opaque mechanics of chip smuggling itself. episodes.description_full: There is something uniquely tragic and terrifying about carbon monoxide poisoning. The way it comes on quietly, without warning. How it alters your reality and changes your behavior. The fact that without a carbon monoxide detector, we can’t smell or taste or see or otherwise sense this poisonous gas. Humans have been dealing with the threat of carbon monoxide poisoning since long before we were a species, and only recently have we developed the skills and knowledge to contend with it. In this episode, we get into the details of carbon monoxide poisoning - why it’s deadly, what symptoms look like, and how we manage cases - before delving into the history of our relationship with the gas. How many ghostly apparitions were actually instances of CO poisoning? What maritime mysteries can be explained by the presence of the gas? And where does carbon monoxide poisoning still remain very much an issue today? Tune in for all the details. episodes.description_full: According to Joshua Goodman, trash collection in New York is one of the last services the city offers that is not yet touched by neoliberalism. What he means is that it's the last free and unlimited city service — there is no opt-in; it is not means tested.
